description: Native combat, action economy, skills, tactical grid, zones of control, melee modes, ranged combat, cover, camouflage, line of sight, large-entity cover, and vehicle combat framework from pages 167-188.

entries.title: Core Combat, Initiative, and Turns
entries.summary: Combat begins with d20 + Initiative, proceeds from highest to lowest result, and normally grants each participant one action per turn without rerolling initiative each round.
body: At combat start, every player and enemy rolls d20 and adds the Initiative statistic. Higher totals act first.

Each participant normally receives one action per turn. Attacking, moving, using an item, and activating a special ability are all examples of actions. Extra actions require an ability, buff, or other specific rule.
After everyone acts, a new round begins. Initiative is not rerolled unless another rule explicitly requires it.

sourceRefs.notes: Initiative, action allocation, turn resolution, and worked example.

entries.title: Native Skills and Action Attribute Pairings
entries.summary: Common actions identify two relevant native attributes, with examples such as STR + DEX for melee and INT + DEX for hacking.
body: The source lists paired relevant attributes for skills and actions. Example text instructs players to roll the paired attributes for Melee Combat, Stealth, Hacking, and Medicine.

This section does not fully define whether every skill always adds both raw attributes, both bonus values, or a primary value plus secondary contribution. That resolution remains a native-system editorial issue.

entries.title: Action Economy, Tactical Grid, and Zones of Control
entries.summary: One-action turns make numerical superiority dangerous; tactical combat uses 5-foot squares, 30-foot standard movement, and adjacent-square zones of control resolved through opposed Strength checks.
body: Action economy measures the number and efficiency of actions available to each side. Being outnumbered exposes a character to multiple enemy actions for each action of their own. Extra actions and effects that delay or remove enemy actions are therefore extremely valuable.
The battlefield uses 5-foot by 5-foot squares. A human-sized entity generally moves 30 feet, or six squares, with a movement action. Faster, injured, and unusual entities adjust this distance.

Every entity controls all adjacent lateral and diagonal squares. Moving through an enemy-controlled square requires opposed Strength checks. The mover proceeds only if their result is higher; the source does not define ties.

entries.title: Close Combat, Wrestling, and Unarmed Combat
entries.summary: The manuscript presents two overlapping melee-resolution descriptions: raw-stat formulas on pages 173-174 and primary-stat bonus selection on page 175.
body: The first description gives direct formulas: Close Combat = STR + DEX - Armor Penalty; Wrestling = STR + DEX; Unarmed Combat = STR + 2 x DEX.

The following page says players choose Strength or Dexterity as the primary statistic, while other relevant statistics contribute partial bonuses ranging from -4 to +4. It retains armor penalties for Close Combat, no armor penalty for Wrestling, and doubled Dexterity benefit for Unarmed Combat.
These are not silently merged. Until a native-system ruling determines precedence, the wiki presents both methods as printed.

entries.title: Ranged Combat, Camouflage, and Cover Economy
entries.summary: Ranged attacks use DEX and INT, technology defines effective range and falloff, camouflage penalizes attacks, and ballistic and energy cover interact differently with weapon types.
body: Ranged attacks roll d20 and add relevant Dexterity and Intelligence contributions. Defensive Value is described as Base DV + Agility Modifiers + Cover Modifiers + Camouflage Modifiers, but Base DV and exact agility conversion are not defined in this section.

Partial cover and partial camouflage each suggest -2 to hit. Full camouflage suggests -4 or complete invisibility depending on conditions. Most ranged weapons suffer -4 at point blank; shotguns and close-quarters weapons are exceptions.

Full cover blocks direct targeting but may be punched through. Ballistic weapons can penetrate ballistic cover at -4; ballistic weapons cannot penetrate energy cover. Energy weapons can penetrate energy cover without penalty but cannot penetrate ballistic barriers according to the later interaction example.
The Advanced Tech range-falloff cell is printed ambiguously as ‘Negligible 50% per 2.’ It is preserved as unresolved source text.

entries.title: Vehicle Combat Framework
entries.summary: Vehicles occupy multiple grid squares, generally move 30 feet per round before modifiers, provide cover, possess armor and Health, and mount weapons whose performance follows technology tiers.
body: Vehicle movement depends on type, technology, terrain, and damage. The general text gives 30 feet per round as a baseline even though the following catalog records vehicle speed in miles per hour; conversion between these measures is not defined here.
Vehicles may provide partial or full cover depending on size and line of sight. Their armor may interact differently with ballistic and energy attacks.

Mounted weapon quality runs from Scavenged and Improvised through Modern, Recovered, Reclaimed, and Advanced Tech. Moving fire may incur accuracy penalties; critical hits can damage individual systems; repairs and maintenance are required.
Detailed vehicle catalogs continue through pages 185-188 and will be imported in the dedicated equipment and vehicle pass rather than flattened into this framework entry.
